title: EUR/SGD settlement can protect principal while leaving cash temporarily unavailable
bank: Deutsche Bundesbank and Monetary Authority of Singapore
summary: Project Simbolon shows how two central banks could protect both sides of a foreign exchange payment without putting their currencies on the same ledger. A common decision bound the euro and Singapore dollar transfers together even when one ledger released its funds later than the other. That distinction matters to a treasury desk. Once the outcome is committed, it can be protected against paying away the principal for nothing and still have no spendable cash in the currency needed for its next obligation. The twelve-week experiment demonstrated the settlement logic with simulated money. The commercial case depends on whether it can release usable liquidity in time, after allowing for prefunding, operating costs and the alternatives available to the banks (executive summary and sections 2–4).

The project involved the Bundesbank and MAS, Deutsche Bank and DBS, and Partior as technology provider. It ran from 10 August to 30 October 2026. The commercial banks held test wallets on both central bank environments. Each central bank controlled its own ledger, assets and settlement requirements. A third ledger coordinated the transaction. The team retained existing bank messaging for the trade instructions and used cryptographic proofs to establish that the settlement conditions had been met. Appendix A places this design alongside earlier shared-platform and linked-infrastructure experiments. A common platform can simplify coordination but requires common operating arrangements. Linking existing systems preserves more local discretion but still requires agreement about which evidence each system will accept. These alternatives were surveyed, without a head-to-head cost or performance trial.

Figure 1 illustrates the funding problem for a European investor buying Singapore securities for next-business-day settlement. Its example has FX booked at 14:00 CET, paired settlement at 19:00 CET or 01:00 Singapore time, and SGD available before the illustrative 10:00 Singapore cash batch. The figure assumes that the allocation is confirmed after the relevant operating window. The FX exchange could then be made closer to the securities deadline. That could shorten the time cash sits idle or reduce a custodian's need to extend credit. The securities delivery against payment is explicitly a future extension. No part of the trial establishes that the investor received securities, reduced a cash buffer by a given amount, or earned the difference between two funding rates (pp. 17–19).

Figure 2 considers a different problem. A bank with spare euros might need Singapore dollars only between two points in the same operating day. An FX swap exchanges currencies and reverses the exchange later, allowing the bank to bridge the temporary imbalance. Each of those exchanges could settle payment-versus-payment. Protection of the two payments within one exchange does not itself supply a counterparty or guarantee that a subsequent funding need can be rolled. The commercial banks remain responsible for liquidity, pricing and execution. The benefit depends on whether a dealer will supply the right amount, at the right time, for less than the cost of prefunding or an outright borrowing facility. The report gives no executable swap price (pp. 20–21).

Figures 3–5 and Appendix B explain how the transaction moves from intention to commitment. The banks match instructions, then each currency is conditionally locked in its own environment. The coordinator verifies evidence of the two locks and records a settlement or abort decision. Each central bank ledger verifies the decision before releasing its currency or refunding it. The proofs establish facts specific to the underlying ledgers. They do not turn a relayer into the owner of the funds, or make the relayer unnecessary. Loss of a supporting service can prevent valid evidence reaching its destination even when it cannot change what that evidence proves. Changing a ledger or settlement contract could also require changes to the proof configuration (tables 4–7 and Appendix E).

Table 2 reports successful settlement, abort and refund, rejection of invalid evidence, handling of duplicate messages, and recovery after an interruption. All produced the expected outcomes. Before a common commitment, a failed exchange can lead to a refund. After commitment, an outstanding release must be completed. Neither party can recover its payment independently after receiving the other currency. This consistency of outcome is valuable even when the releases are recorded at different times. A prolonged interruption, however, would test how long a beneficiary can operate without the money. Timeout and some recovery procedures are described as design provisions. Timeouts were not functionally tested, and some stalled or one-sided locks required manual intervention (section 3.3 and Appendix B.5).

The observed end-to-end time was about five minutes under a fixed configuration. Proof generation accounted for most of it. Table 9 translates that duration into roughly twelve settlements an hour if trades run in sequence. Twelve is arithmetic, not a measured throughput. The table also illustrates what would happen if proof work ran concurrently or were shared across transactions. A batch of 1,000 completed every two to ten minutes implies 6,000–30,000 settlements an hour. Those figures assume the batch size and completion interval. The team did not benchmark that workload. Batching could even delay a particular customer payment while the system waits for other transactions. For a custodian facing a hard cash cutoff, the slowest relevant payments may matter more than the number processed over a full hour (section 4 and Appendix B.7–8).

The distinction between legal and technical finality also survives successful verification. An entry can be final under a ledger's operating rules while the point of irrevocable discharge under the governing law remains unsettled. Appendix C distinguishes coordination by central banks, a contractual arrangement between banks, and operation through a financial market infrastructure. These models would allocate responsibility differently for admitting participants, recognising the final decision and responding to failure. The experiment chose no production model. Its two commercial participants had access to both test environments, while real eligibility for central bank settlement assets would be determined separately in each jurisdiction. A bank lacking direct access might still rely on an intermediary and its hours, limits and credit terms (tables 10–11).

The economic comparison is ultimately between complete funding arrangements. The trial processed individual transactions gross, used no customer money and did not test netting, tokenised deposits or securities delivery. Quicker individual settlement could reduce the time one bank holds an unwanted balance while increasing the need for gross liquidity relative to a netted alternative. That is an inference from the design, and the report supplies no measured sign or size for the net effect. Appendix D identifies the integration, staffing, liquidity access and operating costs that a live business case would have to address. Appendix E records the absence of independent technical assurance, a sustained outage trial and a multi-provider operating test. The investment implication is a question about the cost and reliability of meeting timed cash obligations. The experiment provides no evidence on the direction of EUR/SGD or on how investors price the technology.

questions.question: How much peak liquidity would participants need relative to their current arrangements?
questions.detail: The trial demonstrated coordinated gross transfers. Its use cases suggest shorter holding periods, but there was no netting comparison. Replay the same dated trades and customer deadlines through current settlement and the proposed design. Treasury and custodian records should include peak currency balances, credit-line usage and time spent in escrow. This would reveal whether the saving is a lower peak, a shorter holding period or a redistribution between participants.

questions.question: What happens to a bank's next payment if its currency release is late?
questions.detail: Table 2 establishes the paired outcome following a service restart. Appendix E leaves sustained outages and automated recovery incomplete. Time the interval from commitment to usable funds under high load and interrupted service, then compare its distribution with real payment cutoffs. Operator recovery records, supplemented by a controlled trial, would inform the size of a contingency facility.

questions.question: Would higher throughput improve settlement before the deadline that matters?
questions.detail: The large rates in table 9 are projections. Larger batches may reduce processing cost per payment but leave the first trade waiting. Test realistic, uneven arrivals against sequential processing, reporting completion percentiles, missed cutoffs and fully allocated costs. The data needed are transaction timestamps and measured proof-service capacity under the same workload.

questions.question: Who bears the cost if a technically committed transfer is legally disputed?
questions.detail: Appendix C identifies several possible governance structures. Operational participants cannot budget for failure or set credit limits until the rulebook specifies loss allocation, access and the point of finality in each jurisdiction. Paired legal opinions and draft scheme rules, including insolvency and business-continuity provisions, would help assess the residual exposure.
